questions.q: To whom was Amnon, the son of David, attracted?
questions.a: Amnon loved his beautiful half-sister Tamar, who was the sister of Absalom.

questions.q: How did Amnon respond when Jonadab asked him why he was so weak?
questions.a: Amnon told Jonadab that he loved Tamar, his brother Absalom’s sister.

questions.q: What did Amnon do to get to see Tamar?
questions.a: Amnon pretended to be sick, and when David came to see him, he asked David to let Tamar come and make food for him so he could eat from her hand.

questions.q: What did Amnon do when Tamar came to feed him?
questions.a: When Tamar came to feed him, he seized her and told her to come and lie with him.

questions.q: What did Amnon do when Tamar begged him not to force her?
questions.a: He refused to do what she said he should do. He was stronger than she was, so he forcibly had sexual relations with her.

questions.q: How did Amnon feel toward Tamar after he raped her?
questions.a: Amnon hated her with a very great hatred that was greater than the love with which he had loved her.

questions.q: What did Amnon command Tamar to do?
questions.a: Amnon commanded Tamar to leave.

questions.q: What did Amnon order his servant to do?
questions.a: He ordered his servant to send Tamar outside and to lock the door behind her.

questions.q: What did Tamar do after she was put out of Amnon’s room?
questions.a: Tamar tore the long robe that she was wearing. She put ashes on her head, and she put her hand on her head. As she went away, she kept screaming.

questions.q: What was King David’s response when he heard about these things?
questions.a: When King David heard all these things, it made him very angry, but he did nothing about it.

questions.q: How did Absalom feel toward Amnon after he raped Tamar?
questions.a: Absalom hated Amnon because he had humbled his sister Tamar.

questions.q: Whom did Absalom invite to visit him at Baal Hazor?
questions.a: Absalom invited the king and all the king’s sons to visit him.

questions.q: What did the king say in response to Absalom’s invitation?
questions.a: The king said they should not all go because they would be a heavy burden to Absalom.

questions.q: What did David say when Absalom asked him to let Amnon go with them?
questions.a: But the king replied, “You do not need to invite him to the celebration either.”

questions.q: Who went with Absalom?
questions.a: Absalom urged David, so he sent Amnon and all the king’s sons with him.

questions.q: What did Absalom command his servants to do to Amnon?
questions.a: Absalom commanded his servants to kill Amnon when Amnon began to be drunk with wine.

questions.q: What did the king’s sons do after Absalom’s servants killed Amnon?
questions.a: All the king’s sons arose, and they got onto their mules and escaped by riding away fast.

questions.q: What was the first news David heard about the incident?
questions.a: The first report to David said that Absalom had killed all the king’s sons and not one was still alive.

questions.q: What did Jonadab say had happened and why?
questions.a: Jonadab said that only Amnon is dead. Absalom has been determined to kill him ever since the day that Amnon raped his sister Tamar.

questions.q: Where did Absalom go after having Amnon killed?
questions.a: Absalom fled to Talmai, the son of Ammihud, king of Geshur.

questions.q: How long was Absalom in Geshur?
questions.a: Absalom was in Geshur for three years.

questions.q: What did King David intend to do?
questions.a: King David had intended to attack Absalom and punish him for killing Amnon.

commentary.text: David's grief, Absalom flees to Geshur.

Verses 1–20 From henceforward David was followed with one trouble after another. Adultery and murder were David's sins, the like sins among his children were the beginnings of his punishment: he was too indulgent to his children. Thus David might trace the sins of his children to his own misconduct, which must have made the anguish of the chastisement worse. Let no one ever expect good treatment from those who are capable of attempting their seduction; but it is better to suffer the greatest wrong than to commit the least sin.

Observe the aggravations of Absalom's sin: he would have Ammon slain, when least fit to go out of the world. He engaged his servants in the guilt. Those servants are ill-taught who obey wicked masters, against God's commands. Indulged children always prove crosses to godly parents, whose foolish love leads them to neglect their duty to God.

Jonadab was as guilty of Ammon's death, as of his sin; such false friends do they prove, who counsel us to do wickedly. Instead of loathing Absalom as a murderer, David, after a time, longed to go forth to him. This was David's infirmity: God saw something in his heart that made a difference, else we should have thought that he, as much as Eli, honoured his sons more than God.
